items.title: CVE-2026-109618 Impact of Critical Vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) on Palo Alto Networks Products  (Severity: CRITICAL)
items.one_liner: Active exploitation of critical PHP RCE vulnerabilities targets internet-exposed Palo Alto Networks management interfaces.
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks has evaluated its product portfolio regarding two critical PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which affect PAN-OS software on PA-Series, VM-Series firewalls, and Panorama. CVE-2026-109618 allows RCE via uninitialized request memory after out-of-memory errors handled by longjmp(), while CVE-2026-109619 leaves global memory pointing to freed memory regions. Active exploitation has been observed against management interfaces exposed to the internet, prompting the vendor to assign a critical CVSS score of 9.2 and recommend restricting management access or deploying virtual patches.
key_facts: CVE-2026-109618: CVSS 9.2, remote code execution via OOM longjmp
CVE-2026-109619: remote code execution via global memory pointing to freed regions
items.bottom_line: Administrators must restrict external access to firewall management interfaces immediately to mitigate actively exploited critical PHP vulnerabilities.

items.summary: US authorities report that North Korean state-sponsored hackers have stolen over $400 million in cryptocurrency from more than 900 victims using a social engineering campaign dubbed FaceStealer. items.title: Microsoft Cloud Outage Hits Outlook, Teams, Copilot and AI Services
items.one_liner: A major Microsoft cloud outage took down Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and third-party AI connectors due to unexpected server failures.
items.summary: A massive Microsoft cloud outage disrupted Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and Azure services for thousands of users in the United States and globally on Thursday, November 12. The company paused deployments, redistributed traffic, and worked to bring offline servers back online.

items.title: New SignDrop Zero-Day Exploit Turns Windows CLFS Security Feature Into SYSTEM Access
items.one_liner: A new zero-day Windows CLFS exploit named SignDrop turns security mitigation features into a path for local SYSTEM privilege escalation.
items.summary: A zero-day local privilege escalation exploit named SignDrop has been published by researcher MSNightmare, targeting a log-authentication feature in the Windows Common Log File System (CLFS) driver. The exploit leverages path redirection during companion .cnpf file creation when a privileged process, such as the Windows Defender antimalware service, opens a prepared log file. Independent security researchers confirmed that the attack works on Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025 builds operating under default enforcement configurations, though reliability for operational use varies.
items.bottom_line: Windows systems running default CLFS log authentication enforcement are vulnerable to local privilege escalation via the SignDrop exploit.

items.title: CVE-2026-119618: What We Know About the Critical Apache mod_http2 Race Condition
items.one_liner: Critical HTTP/2 race condition CVE-2026-119618 in Apache allows unauthenticated remote code execution.
items.summary: The Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-119618, a critical race condition in the mod_http2 module affecting Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70. The flaw arises from improper synchronization in the assign_headers() function, leading to heap memory corruption and potential unauthenticated remote code execution. Red Hat reports that public research has demonstrated reliable exploitation against default configurations. The issue is resolved in Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71.

items.title: CVE-2026-0329 PAN-OS: Buffer Overflow Vulnerability (Severity: MEDIUM)
items.one_liner: CVE-2026-0329 exposes Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS firewalls to unauthenticated denial of service attacks via specific certificate or DNS proxy configurations.
items.summary: A buffer overflow vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0329, affects Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS software, enabling an unauthenticated network attacker to trigger a denial of service condition. The flaw impacts firewalls where active IKE Gateway utilizes certificate-based authentication with CRL or OCSP revocation checking enabled, or where a DNS Proxy object is configured. items.bottom_line: Administrators must disable CRL/OCSP revocation checking or DNS proxy objects, or apply threat prevention signatures, to mitigate CVE-2026-0329.

items.title: International operation dismantles malware networks, exposes 6.4 million stolen credentials

items.summary: Police across nine countries dismantled criminal infrastructure associated with the CastleRAT, Gootloader, and StealC malware kits as part of Operation Endgame, seizing 235 servers and 257 domains. Affected victim data will be disseminated through platforms like HaveIBeenPwned and the Shadowserver Foundation for identification and remediation.

items.title: Decision Models in Hugging Face
items.one_liner: A deep dive into decision models that output structured probabilities instead of text tokens for classification tasks.
items.summary: Hugging Face is highlighting decision models, which evaluate options and return probability distributions over predefined answers rather than generating text token by token. These models replace traditional JSON generation workflows to eliminate parsing errors and computational overhead. TypeSafe AI introduced an early iteration named Jev, though the community has settled on the term decision model. The fundamental interface requires a state, questions, and allowed answers to produce decisions with probabilities.
items.bottom_line: Decision models replace brittle JSON text generation with direct probability distributions over predefined answers.

items.title: CVE-2026-126673: Data::Dump::Streamer versions before 3.00 for Perl allow code injection via unescaped Regexp patterns in _dump_qr
items.one_liner: A code injection vulnerability in Data::Dump::Streamer allows arbitrary Perl code execution via crafted Regexp patterns.
items.summary: Data::Dump::Streamer versions before 3.00 for Perl are vulnerable to code injection via unescaped Regexp patterns in the _dump_qr function. Because the pattern is written into a qr literal without proper escaping of '$' or '@', an attacker can inject Perl code that executes when the dump is evaluated. This allows for arbitrary code execution if an application compiles, dumps, and restores data from untrusted sources. Users are advised to upgrade to version 3.00 or avoid restoring dumps containing Regexps from untrusted input.
key_facts: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code
items.bottom_line: Applications using Data::Dump::Streamer to process untrusted data are at risk of RCE and must upgrade to version 3.00.

items.title: Open WebUI: the Windows installer mints the master key from the install second — CVE-2025-15603 was rejected; here is the measurement
items.one_liner: Open WebUI's Windows installer uses a weak, predictable seed for its master secret key, allowing full session token forgery.
items.summary: The Windows installer for Open WebUI generates a master secret key using a linear congruential generator seeded only by the installation time in seconds. This flaw allows an attacker to recover the master key in approximately 2.1 seconds, enabling the forgery of administrator session tokens. Despite being reported as CVE-2025-15603, the vendor disputed the finding and rejected the CVE, claiming no action was required. New research confirms the vulnerability persists across all 178 release tags, with most lacking even basic per-account session stamps.
key_facts: Vulnerability: Predictable master secret key generation
items.bottom_line: Administrators should assume all Open WebUI installations on Windows are compromised and rotate all secrets immediately.

items.title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
items.one_liner: LLMON is an XML-like markup language designed to defeat prompt injection and replace brittle JSON parsing in LLMs.
items.summary: Researchers have introduced LLMON (LLM Object Notation), an LLM-native markup language designed to replace JSON for causal language models by using reserved special-token delimiters for explicit structure and data binding. By wrapping semantic components in tags and mapping unique identifiers to instructions, the format prevents indirect prompt injections and stops models from pulling unrelated context into answers. IBM has released two experimental preview models based on Granite 4.1 (3B and 8B parameters) trained natively on LLMON, alongside a GitHub toolkit for conversions and workflows.
items.bottom_line: Adopting LLMON and its supporting Granite models eliminates indirect prompt injection risks by explicitly binding instructions to data payloads.

items.title: Signed, Sealed, and Relayed, NTLM-style: Bypassing LDAP Signing Through Reauthentication
items.one_liner: NTLM relay bypass against enforced LDAP signing exposes Windows Server 2016-2025 to complete domain compromise.
items.summary: SpecterOps researchers discovered a vulnerability (CVE-2026-70229) allowing NTLM relay attacks against LDAP connections even when LDAP signing is enforced. By establishing a signed connection, capturing a valid session key, and relaying a victim's NTLM authentication into an existing SASL record, attackers can execute malicious LDAP commands with the victim's privileges. This bypass affects all Windows Server versions from 2016 to 2025 and permits complete domain compromise via computer takeover primitives. Microsoft released a patch for the LDAP variant in October 2026 following an independent patch for SMB in September 2026.
items.bottom_line: NTLM authentication can be successfully relayed over existing signed LDAP connections, bypassing signing protections and enabling full domain compromise.

items.summary: Volexity detected spear-phishing campaigns in September 2026 by Chinese threat actors UTA0560 and JungleBamboo targeting NGOs using a multi-stage exploit chain. The attacks abused reflected XSS on legitimate websites to redirect victims to a Google Chrome zero-day, CVE-2026-85046, which was unpatched in released browser versions despite upstream fixes in Chromium. The exploit chain leveraged a V8 type-confusion bug (CVE-2026-85046), a WebAssembly sandbox escape (CVE-2026-87491), and a Windows kernel vulnerability (CVE-2026-85880) to deploy malware including the GRIMWEDGE backdoor and SUPERSTOMP loader.
items.bottom_line: Threat actors UTA0560 and JungleBamboo have been observed chaining a Chrome zero-day (CVE-2026-85046) and Windows kernel bug to target NGOs with persistent backdoors.

items.title: Agent Substrate: Advancing Kubernetes for Agents at Scale
items.one_liner: Agent Substrate is a CNCF Sandbox runtime designed to scale Kubernetes for idle-heavy AI agents.
items.summary: Agent Substrate is an open-source, zero-trust runtime donated to the CNCF Sandbox to address Kubernetes' inefficiencies when running autonomous AI agents and coding assistants at scale. Because traditional Kubernetes Pod lifecycles introduce multi-second cold starts and hold idle memory, Agent Substrate multiplexes many agent sessions across a smaller pool of persistent worker Pods. Idle sessions are snapshotted—including memory and filesystems via gVisor or microVMs—and restored onto available workers without hitting the API server or scheduler. This architecture achieves tenfold higher density and eliminates the latency overhead of turning agent steps into ephemeral containers.
key_facts: Density improvement: 10x higher density than standard containers
items.bottom_line: Agent Substrate solves the container cold-start and memory overhead problem for AI agents on Kubernetes by checkpointing and multiplexing sessions over worker pools.

claims.support_span: Agent Substrate, now donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox, is an open-source, security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers.

items.title: Backporting security fixes at scale with Codex
items.one_liner: AI-assisted backporting is proving to be a viable solution for the massive, often neglected backlog of security patches in stable Linux distributions.
items.summary: Trail of Bits is utilizing an AI-driven tool called Codex to automate the backporting of security fixes for stable Linux kernel releases and major distributions like Ubuntu and Fedora. By using agents to identify missing patches, adapt them to older codebases, and assemble validation evidence, the project has reduced the human effort required for backporting from days to hours. As of October 29, the project successfully delivered fixes for 149 distinct CVEs into stable releases. This initiative aims to bridge the gap between security and stability for users who rely on long-term support versions of software.
items.bottom_line: AI-driven automation is successfully reducing the time and effort required to backport critical security fixes to stable software, making it feasible to secure long-term support releases.

items.one_liner: A multi-stage supply-chain attack used poisoned npm packages to steal developer credentials, leading to the compromise of Nx Console and internal GitHub repositories.
items.summary: A sophisticated supply-chain attack compromised TanStack packages by chaining three vulnerabilities in their GitHub Actions workflow, allowing the attacker to publish malicious versions to npm. items.title: PoC Exploit Released for Critical Cisco Expressway RCE Vulnerability With CVSS 9.8 Score
items.one_liner: A public PoC exploit for CVE-2026-76466 lets attackers achieve root RCE on clustered Cisco Expressway deployments via hard-coded credentials.
items.summary: A public proof-of-concept exploit and fleet detector have been released for CVE-2026-76466, a critical CVSS 9.8 vulnerability in Cisco Expressway. The flaw stems from hard-coded credentials and a hard-coded maintenance identity in the cluster-manager module's cm_server, allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary commands as root via TCP port 4372. Clustered Expressway-C and Expressway-E deployments are affected when running in factory-default TLS Permissive mode. Cisco has urged administrators to upgrade to fixed releases such as X15.5.20 or restrict access to ports 4371 and 4372 as no direct workaround exists.

items.title: Screen Eavesdropping Over the Air: Open-Source Deep-TEMPEST Tool on GitHub Uses AI to Read HDMI Cable Signals - Andro-News
items.one_liner: Deep-TEMPEST lets attackers passively reconstruct text from HDMI cable RF emissions using SDRs and PyTorch, bypassing air-gapped security.
items.summary: Researchers at the University of the Republic in Montevideo published Deep-TEMPEST on GitHub, an open-source tool that uses Software-Defined Radio (SDR) and deep learning to reconstruct live monitor output from unintended radio emissions leaking out of ordinary HDMI cables. Operating completely passively and without network access or malware, the tool tunes into the third pixel harmonic (such as 324 MHz in 1600x900 tests) using hardware like HackRF, passes raw frames through GNU Radio and the DRUNet PyTorch architecture for denoising, and applies Tesseract OCR. This pipeline reduces the character error rate from gr-tempest's 90% down to under 30%, making onscreen text legible to humans or language models from afar.
key_facts: Center frequency: 324 MHz (third harmonic of pixel clock in 1600x900 tests)
items.bottom_line: Deep-TEMPEST demonstrates that deep learning and SDRs can passively read monitor output via stray HDMI cable radio emissions with under 30% character error.

items.title: CVE-2026-128066 - Pillow: Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
items.one_liner: A memory DoS vulnerability in Pillow < 13.0.0 allows crafted TIFF and EXIF data to trigger quadratic memory exhaustion.
items.summary: A memory denial-of-service vulnerability exists in Python imaging library Pillow versions 1.0 through 12.3.0 within ImageFileDirectory_v2.load() in TiffImagePlugin.py. items.title: CVE-2026-68548 - Algernon: Case-insensitive filesystem lets unauthenticated requests bypass /admin,/repo,/data permission-prefix gate
items.one_liner: Algernon web server prior to v1.17.10 suffers from an unauthenticated permission bypass on case-insensitive filesystems via mixed-case URL paths.
items.summary: A vulnerability designated as CVE-2026-68548 affects Algernon, a pure-Go web server prior to version 1.17.10. The flaw stems from a mismatch where the URL-prefix authorization gate performs case-sensitive checks for protected prefixes like /admin, /repo, and /data, while file system path resolution is case-insensitive. On systems utilizing case-insensitive filesystems like Windows NTFS or macOS APFS/HFS+, attackers can send mixed-case requests to completely bypass permission prefix gates. This unauthenticated bypass enables unauthorized reading and execution of protected files. The issue has been patched in version 1.17.10.
key_facts: Affected Software: Algernon prior to version 1.17.10
items.bottom_line: Running Go web applications with prefix-based access controls on case-insensitive filesystems risks severe authorization bypasses.

items.one_liner: A heap use-after-free in VVdeC allows for potential denial of service via crafted VVC bitstreams.

items.summary: A preliminary investigation into the Kolkata-Sairang Express derailment in Assam indicates a malfunctioning main braking system. The probe team found that the BP angle cock, which controls coach brakes, was in an isolated (closed) position in the locomotive, preventing the brakes from engaging. While the train crew claimed the system was functional at the start of the journey, it is suspected that the valve was closed during a maintenance stop to address jammed brake pads and never reopened. A formal investigation is ongoing to determine if this was a procedural oversight or human error.

items.title: AI Security Assessment: A Six-Step Full-Stack Evaluation Standard
items.one_liner: A credible full-stack AI security assessment must pair adversarial model testing with traditional web, API, and cloud vulnerability evaluations.
items.summary: Bishop Fox published an AI security assessment framework arguing that shallow automated scans miss critical risks where AI model outputs turn into database queries, API calls, and agent actions. items.title: YuanKong RAT: the Android remote-control service that stamps its operators' names into every build
items.one_liner: YuanKong Android RAT analysis shows how hardcoded operator handles and weak XOR encryption allow researchers to expose complete operator rosters.
items.summary: StarLabs SG published a technical teardown of YuanKong, a multi-tenant Android remote-control service (RAT) that embeds operator identifiers directly into its builds. Analysis of 110 droppers revealed a self-describing vault-config.json file containing plaintext keys that decrypt a ZIP containing the payload. The payload shares a single signing certificate across 57 distinct variants while baking unique operator accounts, handles, and enrollment codes into the DEX constants. The malware reports these owner details back to its C2 on every foreground-app event, allowing analysts to map entire operator rosters from a single sample.
items.bottom_line: YuanKong Android RAT builds contain hardcoded operator credentials and cleartext configuration files, enabling attribution and roster extraction from single binaries.

items.title: How I Found a $113,337 AF_ALG Linux Local Privilege Escalation Before Copy Fail
items.one_liner: A retrospective look at uncovering a $113,337 Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw in the AF_ALG cryptographic subsystem via unprivileged socket APIs.
items.summary: Security researcher Muhammad Alifa Ramdhan details the discovery of CVE-2025-39964, a critical race condition vulnerability in the Linux kernel's AF_ALG cryptographic subsystem that earned a $113,337 reward via Google's kernelCTF. Exploiting out-of-bounds access stemming from how AF_ALG handles inputs across unprivileged sockets, an ordinary user can escalate privileges to root or achieve container escape. Present in the kernel since 2011, this vulnerability preceded the widely known 'Copy Fail' flaw but highlights the same underlying kernel attack surface.
items.bottom_line: Unprivileged access to the Linux kernel's AF_ALG subsystem harbors deep race condition vulnerabilities capable of full privilege escalation and container escape.

items.title: The School Bomb Threats Came From Accounts Already in Stolen Data
items.one_liner: Historical infostealer data is being repurposed to facilitate large-scale hoax campaigns, underscoring the long-term risk of credential exposure.
items.summary: Recent bomb threats sent to thousands of European schools have been linked to stolen credentials found in infostealer data. Hudson Rock researchers identified that two university email addresses used in the threats appeared in historical infostealer logs, some dating back over five years. While the threats were hoaxes, the incident highlights how compromised credentials from old infections can be leveraged for malicious activity. The researchers emphasize that the presence of these addresses in stolen data does not necessarily implicate the account holders as the perpetrators.
items.bottom_line: Old, leaked credentials remain a potent tool for attackers to conduct disruptive campaigns, even years after the initial infection.

items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>

items.summary: A flaw in Git can let a malicious repository run an attacker's code on a computer that clones it recursively, together with its submodules. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-111760, is an integer truncation in how Git handles its index. An extremely long path in a repository can pass Git's safety check, but Git then writes it to disk under a shorter name that an attacker can set to .git. This lets an attacker replace a submodule's .git file with a symbolic link to a folder holding malicious hooks or configuration.

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude

items.summary: Faced with a mysterious, intermittently beeping device buried in a box room, software developer Simon Willison used Claude Code to build 'Beep Locator,' a software system that triangulates the source of acoustic signals using multiple commodity devices. Running on a Python web server with client interfaces connected via WebSockets, the app utilizes device-to-device audio ranging inspired by the 2007 research paper 'BeepBeep' by Chunyi Peng et al. items.one_liner: AI security scoping must align specific testing methodologies—from pen testing to red teaming—with concrete risk decisions across the full stack.
items.summary: Effective AI security scoping requires organizations to define the specific risk decision—such as shipping, gating, expanding, or mitigating—before selecting an appropriate evaluation method. items.bottom_line: Treating AI evaluations as a generic check leaves multi-layered enterprise AI deployments vulnerable; scoping must match specific risk decisions.

items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. items.title: We Built An Agent That Broke All of Our Security Rules. Here's What We Learned.
items.summary: We tell customers three things about securing AI agents: they need their own identities, access that fits the job they’re given, and traceability that’s separate from any human’s. Then, we built an agent that broke all three by default. This helped us think through how such agents should be defended. When a browser agent acts inside a user’s authenticated session, the application may see the user but not the agent, the delegation, or the task’s intended scope. By creating an agent that breaks all the security rules, Token learned how companies should be using identity to gain control, especially as agent use scales.

items.title: How reliable are AI coding tools? A new test focuses on each model's limits.
items.summary: When AI companies release new models, they often tout their scores on standardized tests called benchmarks. But traditional benchmark methodologies have recently faced questions about reliability from AI researchers as well as the companies that make the models. One reason for those doubts is that existing benchmarks can sometimes conceal big differences between models. For example, on one popular coding benchmark, DeepSWE, models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and DeepSeek all score within a point of each other. But when the same models were tested on a new benchmark, the gap between them grew to nearly 35 points, separating models that had looked evenly matched.
